text: Solari Vision Labs needs a bigger GPU training cluster for its next defect-detection model retrain, and right now it has zero GPU nodes in its Kubernetes cluster. This lab builds that cluster from nothing, in six numbered steps, pulling directly on the instance selection, Terraform provisioning, driver setup, and Kubernetes scheduling you've already learned across Chapters 1 and 2.

Step one checks the Standard NC A100 v4 quota in the target region before writing a single resource block. Step two provisions six of those GPU VMs with Terraform, but each one's custom_data bootstrap script does two jobs in a single pass: it installs the NVIDIA driver and Container Toolkit, then runs the kubeadm join command, so a node only finishes booting once it's genuinely ready for GPU work and already a member of the cluster.

Step three re-runs the nvidia-smi and docker --gpus all smoke test from Chapter 2 against each real new node. Step four labels all six nodes accelerator=nvidia-a100, taints them so ordinary pods can't land there, and deploys the NVIDIA device plugin -- the label pulls GPU workloads in, the taint keeps everything else out, and neither one alone is enough.

Step five confirms the payoff: kubectl describe node should now show nvidia.com/gpu as real capacity on every worker. If any node reports zero, the fix is checking that node's device plugin pod logs first, not re-provisioning the VM. Quota, Terraform, drivers, and Kubernetes scheduling all have to line up correctly for that single number to appear.

Step six is the real proof: a training Job requesting four GPUs, with a node selector and toleration matching what step four just configured, actually reaching the Running state on real hardware. That's the difference between each piece technically working in isolation and a cluster that's genuinely ready to train a production model.

With a working GPU training cluster now provisioned end to end, Lesson 30 moves to the other side of the ML lifecycle: deploying an autoscaling model-serving endpoint for a trained model, one that scales to zero when idle and scales up on GPU utilization instead of running expensive GPUs around the clock for no traffic.
